title: Slow upload speed for http server
body: I tested uploads of 10 MB, 100 MB, and 1 GB files to a localhost HTTP server. My Deno server streams req.body to a file, but it is about 2–3x slower than my Node.js server for the smaller files. With a 1 GB file, Deno takes between 20 seconds and 5 minutes, uses almost all CPU on my Ubuntu 20.04 VPS with 2 CPU cores and 2 GB RAM, and becomes progressively slower over repeated uploads. Node takes about 1–1.7 seconds and remains stable. I create the test files with truncate and upload them with curl --data-binary.

symptoms_visible: My Deno upload server takes 60–90 ms for 10 MB, 500–600 ms for 100 MB, and between 20 seconds and 5 minutes for 1 GB, while Node takes about 35–40 ms, 260 ms, and 1–1.7 seconds respectively.
Repeated 1 GB uploads become slower each time and use almost all CPU on my two-core VPS; the Node upload time stays stable.
N0.label: N0 severe upload slowdown reported

symptoms_visible: Repeated 1 GB uploads to the Deno server become progressively slower and consume nearly all available CPU, while the Node server remains stable.
N1.label: N1 comparison implementation collected

symptoms_visible: With Deno 1.19 and req.body.pipeTo(file.writable), a 1 GB upload now takes about 5.3 seconds instead of 16.5 seconds and repeated results are more stable, but Node takes 2.3 seconds and uses about half as much CPU.
N2_x.label: N2_x native file Web Stream aftermath

symptoms_visible: On a second VPS with four CPUs and 8 GB RAM, Deno writes the 1 GB upload at about 200 MB/s while Node reaches about 450 MB/s.
Across later Deno and standard-library versions through Deno 1.24, the 1 GB Deno upload remains around twice as slow as Node.
N3.label: N3 hardware and version dependence checked

symptoms_visible: After changing the server to Deno.serve on Deno 1.25, the 1 GB upload remains about twice as slow as the Node server.
N3_x.label: N3_x Deno.serve aftermath

symptoms_visible: In my additional test, sending a 512 MB buffer takes 4687 ms from the browser and 2947 ms on the Deno side to open and save the file.
N4.label: N4 upload profile collected

symptoms_visible: On Deno 1.34.3, a 1 GB upload takes 2.7 seconds on my four-core VPS while Node takes 1.8 seconds.
N5_x.label: N5_x newer release aftermath

symptoms_visible: With both runtimes tested through the same native-stream API, repeated 1 GB uploads complete in approximately the same time; the progressive slowdown and CPU-saturation behavior no longer occurs.
N_terminal.label: terminal equivalent APIs benchmarked

question_patterns: Can you share the Node server code used for the comparison?
How does the Node implementation stream the request body to disk?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: My Node server is an Express route that creates an fs.WriteStream and runs await stream.pipeline(req, fs_stream) before sending the response.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: My Node comparison also converts the request and file streams to Web Streams and connects them with pipeTo.
The Node route uses the same native stream.pipeline call but writes to a different filename.

question_patterns: Which Deno and Node versions are you testing?
Is there anything else about the test machine needed to reproduce the result?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I'm using the latest Deno available at the time and Node 16. The server has two CPUs and 2 GB RAM. Please try uploading the 1 GB file repeatedly, because each run gets slower.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The server has the same amount of RAM but uses a different hostname.

edges.comment: Comments c0-c8: the reporter supplies the Node implementation and reiterates the constrained VPS environment, CPU use, and repeat-dependent slowdown.

solution.intent: Upgrade to the release with native Web Streams on files and pipe the request body directly to file.writable instead of using the standard-library writer adapter.
solution.concrete_example: Create the file with Deno.create and run await req.body.pipeTo(file.writable).

edges.comment: Comments c11-c13: direct file.writable use produces a major improvement and stabilizes repeated uploads, but the reporter still measures 5.3 seconds versus Node's 2.3 seconds. It is therefore not the complete explanation for the remaining comparison gap.

question_patterns: Can you repeat the direct file.writable benchmark on a machine with more CPU and memory?
Does the remaining gap persist on the larger VPS?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran it on another VPS with four CPUs and 8 GB RAM and got the same result: Deno is about 200 MB/s and Node about 450 MB/s for the 1 GB upload.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: On the larger VPS, Deno and Node complete the same upload in effectively identical times.
The larger VPS gives 210 MB/s for Deno and 440 MB/s for Node.

question_patterns: Does the result change on subsequent Deno and standard-library releases?
Can you retest after updating Deno?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I retested releases from Deno 1.19.2 through 1.24 with their current standard-library versions. Individual times vary a little, but Deno remains around twice as slow as Node.

edges.comment: Comments c14-c22: the reporter establishes that the residual gap is not specific to the two-core VPS or one short-lived release.

solution.intent: Replace the standard-library HTTP server with Deno.serve while continuing to pipe the Web request body to the file's writable stream.
solution.concrete_example: Run the same handler under Deno.serve and keep await req.body.pipeTo(file.writable) as the upload path.

edges.comment: Comment c24: the reporter tested Deno.serve and observed the same roughly twofold comparison gap. Merely changing the HTTP server entry point does not remove the Web Streams cost.

question_patterns: Can you profile a large upload and report the raw client and server timings?
Please record the upload with the JavaScript profiler and share the measured duration.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I sent a 512 MB buffer from the browser. It took 4687 ms from start to finish in the browser and 2947 ms on the Deno side to open and save the file.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The profile contains almost no JavaScript execution during the transfer, and the server-side file save finishes at native-stream speed.

question_patterns: Can you share the performance recording for one upload, including a zoomed-in view?
What does the profiler timeline look like during the upload?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I've attached the performance graph for one upload and a zoomed-in view of the same recording.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I captured the same pattern with a 1 GB upload instead of a 512 MB upload.

edges.comment: Comments c36-c39: profiling and raw timings came from another affected participant, folded into the simulated user side. The participant wondered whether the fast path was active, but that interpretation is not placed in the user's answer.

solution.intent: Update to a substantially newer Deno release and repeat the existing Deno.serve plus file.writable benchmark.
solution.concrete_example: Retest the same 1 GB upload after upgrading Deno while leaving the Web Streams implementation unchanged.

edges.comment: Comment c41: later releases improve the absolute result to 2.7 seconds versus 1.8 seconds, but updating alone does not make the unlike-API benchmark equal.

solution.intent: Correct the benchmark and performance-sensitive implementation by comparing the same stream API on both runtimes: use native Node-compatible streams under Deno when maximum throughput is required, or compare Web Streams against Web Streams. The remaining apparent runtime gap comes from comparing Deno Web Streams with Node native streams, not from slower Deno socket or file I/O.
solution.concrete_example: Benchmark node:http plus native fs streams and stream.pipeline on both Node and Deno, using the same curl -T upload. If the application must use Deno.serve, compare it with a Node Web Streams implementation rather than Node's native pipeline. Please repeat several 1 GB uploads with the matched implementation and report the timings and CPU behavior before considering the issue resolved.
solution.inference_hint: The final maintainer reran a 2×2 benchmark matrix. Native node:http and filesystem streams took about 0.52 seconds on Node and 0.57 seconds on Deno; Web Streams took about 1.05 seconds on Node and 0.76 seconds on Deno, while Deno.serve plus file.writable took about 0.80 seconds. Deriving that the runtime I/O gap disappears under a matched API, and that the remaining cost belongs to the Web Streams abstraction, is engineer-side analysis rather than a fact the reporter supplied.

edges.comment: Final accepted diagnosis in c43: the catastrophic historical behavior is no longer reproducible, and the persistent approximately twofold claim came from comparing different stream abstractions. The technical resolution is an API-matched benchmark or use of native Node-compatible streams in Deno, not another Deno.serve/file.writable rewrite.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause: the original benchmark compares Deno's Web Streams upload path with Node's native stream.pipeline path, so the residual difference is primarily Web Streams abstraction overhead rather than slower Deno socket or filesystem I/O.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected implementations, repeated large-file timings, cross-machine tests, and profiling evidence, together with a same-API benchmark; it must not be asserted from the initial timing alone.
Must recommend an apples-to-apples comparison: native streams on both runtimes or Web Streams on both runtimes, with Node-compatible native streams under Deno as the maximum-throughput option.
Must not present direct file.writable use, switching to Deno.serve, or merely updating Deno while retaining the unlike-API benchmark as a complete fix; each was tried and the measured gap remained.
Must distinguish the old catastrophic progressive slowdown and CPU saturation from the later residual stream-API cost; the former was no longer reproducible in the final investigation.
Must ask the user to verify repeated large uploads, timings, and CPU behavior with a matched stream API before declaring the issue resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Technically capable server-side developer who can write equivalent Deno and Node upload handlers, run repeatable curl benchmarks on multiple VPS machines, upgrade runtimes, and follow profiling instructions.
persona_hint.communication_style: Direct and persistent; reports concrete versions and timings, repeatedly retests new releases, and emphasizes practical throughput and CPU differences.
